title: Social Media Marketing for Business
subtitle: Plan, post, advertise and measure on Facebook, Instagram, TikTok and WhatsApp so your social media brings real customers and sales.
description: A practical course for Nigerian and African small businesses. You will choose the right platforms, set up business profiles and Meta Business Suite, create posts and Reels that people respond to, run small paid ads with clear naira budgets, and measure what actually brings in sales. Every lesson ends with a task you complete for your own business.
outcomes: Choose the right platforms for your customers and set up business profiles, Meta Business Suite and WhatsApp Business
Plan, create and schedule a month of posts, Reels and Stories using content pillars
Turn comments and messages into orders with a clear customer service routine
Run a small Click-to-WhatsApp or boosted ad with a naira budget and judge whether it is profitable
Read Insights, track enquiries and sales, and write a 90-day social media plan
audience: Women running or starting small businesses who already use social media personally and want it to bring in customers.
tools: A smartphone with a working camera and data
Facebook, Instagram and WhatsApp Business apps (TikTok optional)
Meta Business Suite (free app or business.facebook.com)
Free editing apps such as CapCut and Canva
A notebook or spreadsheet for tracking enquiries and sales
Optional: a small ad budget, for example 10,000 to 20,000 naira (approximate) for a first test

modules.title: Platform Strategy and Audience Building
modules.overview: Choose the platforms where your buyers already spend time, set up business profiles that make it easy to buy, understand how each feed decides who sees your posts, and grow a real audience without paying for followers.

lessons.title: Choosing the right platforms for your Nigerian customers
objectives: Describe your ideal customer in one clear sentence
Compare Facebook, Instagram, TikTok, WhatsApp, X and LinkedIn for business use
Choose one main platform and one support platform for your business
Explain why being on fewer platforms done well beats being everywhere

blocks.text: Social media marketing is simply using social platforms to help the right people find your business, trust it and buy from it. The first decision is not what to post. It is **where** to post. Every platform has a different crowd, a different style of content and different business tools. A small business with one or two people cannot do all of them well, so the skill is choosing.
Start with your customer, not the app

Before you look at any platform, write one sentence about your best customer: who she is, where she lives, what she needs and how she likes to buy. For example: "Working mothers in Lagos aged 28 to 45 who want ready-to-cook soup ingredients delivered on Saturday." This sentence is your **target audience**. Every choice in this course goes back to it.

items: **Who:** age range, gender if it matters, job or life stage
**Where:** city or area you can actually deliver to or serve
**Need:** the problem your product or service solves for her
**Buying habit:** does she buy after seeing photos, after chatting, after watching a demo, or after a friend recommends you?

blocks.name: target-audience
blocks.alt: A person aiming at a target made of customer profiles
blocks.caption: Describe your target customer first, then choose the platform she already uses.

blocks.text: What each platform is good for

head: Platform
Main content style
Strong business tools
Often suits
rows: Pages, Groups, Marketplace, Meta Business Suite, ads
Local services, adult buyers, community selling, events
Professional account, Insights, Story links, ads
Fashion, beauty, food, crafts, anything visual
Business account, analytics, Promote, TikTok Ads Manager
Products you can demonstrate, younger buyers, entertainment-style teaching
Catalogue, quick replies, labels, greeting and away messages
Closing sales and customer service for almost every small business

blocks.text: Notice that WhatsApp is different from the rest. Facebook, Instagram and TikTok help people **discover** you. WhatsApp is where most Nigerian small businesses **close** the sale: the customer asks the price, sends a delivery address and confirms payment. So for most businesses, WhatsApp Business is not a choice, it is the cash register, and the real decision is which discovery platform feeds it.
The one main, one support rule

Pick **one main platform** where you post regularly and learn deeply, and **one support platform** where you share the best of the same content. Add WhatsApp Business as your sales channel. Only add a third platform when the first two run smoothly every week. Posting once a month on five platforms looks abandoned; posting four times a week on one looks alive.

blocks.title: From choice to sale
items: Describe target customer
Pick main platform
Add support platform
Send chats to WhatsApp
Review after 30 days
blocks.caption: Platforms are chosen from the customer outward, and every platform should lead buyers to one place where you close sales.

blocks.title: Worked example: choosing platforms for a small catering business
blocks.context: For example, Funmi runs a small-chops and party-tray business in Ibadan. Her best customers are women aged 30 to 55 who organise birthdays, church events and office parties. She has one phone and about 5 hours a week for marketing.
steps: She writes her customer sentence: "Event organisers in Ibadan who want reliable, tasty small chops delivered on time."
She notes her customers mostly ask friends for recommendations and look at photos of past events before ordering.
She chooses Facebook as her main platform, because her customers are active in local Facebook groups and she can post event photos and reviews there.
She chooses Instagram as her support platform and shares the same photos and short videos there, linked to Facebook through Meta Business Suite so one post can go to both.
She puts her WhatsApp Business link on both profiles so every enquiry lands in one inbox.
blocks.result: Funmi spends her 5 hours on two connected platforms instead of five, and all her orders arrive in one WhatsApp inbox she can track.

blocks.text: Questions to test your choice

items: Can I create the kind of content this platform rewards at least three times a week? TikTok needs video; LinkedIn needs written ideas; Instagram needs good pictures.
Do my customers use this platform to buy, or only to be entertained?
Can I reply to messages on it every day, or will enquiries be missed?
Does it have tools I need, such as a catalogue, scheduling or local ads?

blocks.text: If you answer "no" to two or more of these for a platform, it is probably not your main platform yet. You can still reserve your business name on it so nobody else takes it, and come back later when you have more time or help.

blocks.title: Check where your competitors win
blocks.text: Search for three businesses like yours in your city. Note which platform gets them the most comments and real questions, not just likes. That is a strong clue about where your buyers are.

blocks.title: Your personal page is not a business page
blocks.text: Selling only from a personal Facebook profile works at the start, but you lose business tools such as Insights, ads, scheduling and a separate business inbox. Set up proper business accounts in the next lesson.

takeaways: Write your target customer sentence before choosing any platform
Discovery platforms bring people in; WhatsApp Business usually closes the sale
Use one main platform and one support platform until both run smoothly
Review your choice after 30 days using real enquiries, not likes

activity.title: Choose your platforms
steps: Write your target customer sentence using the four points: who, where, need, buying habit.
Look at three similar businesses in your city and note which platform brings them the most real questions.
Choose your main platform and your support platform, and write one reason for each.
Confirm you have WhatsApp Business installed (not the ordinary WhatsApp) on your business number.
activity.evidence: A note with your customer sentence, the three competitors you checked, and your chosen platforms with reasons.

lessons.title: Setting up business profiles that make people buy
objectives: Convert a personal Instagram or TikTok account to a professional or business account
Write a bio that says what you sell, where, and how to order
Connect your Facebook Page and Instagram account in Meta Business Suite
Set up WhatsApp Business with a catalogue, greeting message and quick replies

blocks.text: A stranger decides in a few seconds whether your profile looks like a real, trustworthy business. Your profile is your shop front. It must answer four questions quickly: **What do you sell? Where? Can I trust you? How do I order?** If any of these is missing, people scroll away.
Switch to business tools

items: **Facebook:** create a Facebook Page for the business (separate from your personal profile). Choose a category such as "Caterer" or "Clothing store".
**Instagram:** in Settings, switch to a **professional account** and choose **Business** (best for selling) or Creator. This unlocks Insights, contact buttons and ads.
**TikTok:** in Settings, switch to a **Business account**. You get analytics and can add a website link once eligible.
**WhatsApp Business:** a separate free app from Meta. Use your business number and fill in the business profile, hours, address and catalogue.

blocks.name: social-bio
blocks.alt: A phone showing a social media profile with a photo and bio
blocks.caption: A clear photo, name and bio tell a visitor in seconds what you sell and how to order.

blocks.text: The parts of a strong profile

head: Part
What to do
Common mistake
rows: Use the business name plus a keyword, for example "Ada's Ankara | Abuja"
Handles with many numbers and underscores that are hard to type
Clear logo or a bright face photo, readable at small size
Tiny text logo nobody can read on a phone
What you sell, where, a proof point, and how to order
Quotes and emojis with no information
WhatsApp link, phone, email, location if you have a shop
"DM for price" with no other way to reach you
Prices or menu, reviews, how to order, delivery areas

blocks.text: A good bio formula is: **I help [who] get [result] with [product], in [place]. [Proof]. Order: [how].** You have about 150 characters on Instagram, so every word must work. Put your WhatsApp click-to-chat link in the link space. The format is wa.me followed by your number in international form without the plus sign or leading zero, for example wa.me/2348012345678 (an illustrative number).
Connect everything in Meta Business Suite

**Meta Business Suite** is Meta's free tool (app and website at business.facebook.com) that puts your Facebook Page and Instagram account in one place. From it you can post to both at once, schedule posts, answer Facebook and Instagram messages and comments in one inbox, and see Insights. Connect your Instagram account to your Page in the Page settings or inside Business Suite, then set up automatic replies for common questions.

blocks.title: Profile ready checklist
items: Business account switched on
Clear photo and name
Bio with how to order
WhatsApp link added
Pinned prices and reviews
Business Suite connected
blocks.caption: Tick every item before you start posting regularly, so new visitors can act on what they see.

blocks.title: Worked example: rewriting a weak bio
blocks.context: For example, Ada sells ready-made Ankara dresses from her home in Abuja. Her old Instagram bio said: "God's own designer. Blessed. DM for enquiries."
steps: She switches her Instagram to a Business account and picks the category "Clothing (brand)".
She changes her name field to "Ada's Ankara | Abuja" so it appears in searches for Ankara and Abuja.
She rewrites the bio: "Ready-to-wear Ankara dresses for work and owambe. Sizes 8 to 20. Delivery across Abuja. Order on WhatsApp below."
She adds her wa.me link and creates three Story Highlights: Price list, Reviews, How to order.
In WhatsApp Business she adds 12 dresses to the catalogue with prices and a greeting message: "Thank you for contacting Ada's Ankara. Send the dress name and your size."
blocks.result: A visitor now knows what Ada sells, for whom, in which sizes, where she delivers and exactly how to order, without asking a single question first.

blocks.text: Common profile mistakes to fix today

items: **Different names on every platform.** Use the same name and, if possible, the same handle everywhere so customers can find you and trust that it is really you.
**No prices anywhere.** You do not have to list every price, but a "from" price or a price list Highlight saves time and filters out people who cannot afford you.
**Out-of-date information.** Old phone numbers, closed shop addresses and expired offers make you look inactive. Check your profiles on the first day of each month.
**A private account.** A business account must be public so that new people can see your posts.

blocks.text: Ask a friend who has never seen your page to look at it for ten seconds, then tell you what you sell, where and how to order. If they cannot answer all three, your profile still needs work. This simple test is one of the fastest ways to find gaps you cannot see yourself.

blocks.title: Protect your accounts
blocks.text: Turn on two-factor authentication on Facebook, Instagram, TikTok and WhatsApp. Never share login codes with anyone who messages you, even if they claim to be Meta support or offer you a verified badge. Account takeovers of Nigerian business pages often start with a fake support message.

blocks.title: Use quick replies
blocks.text: In WhatsApp Business, save quick replies for your price list, delivery fees and payment details. Typing a slash brings them up, which saves time and keeps your answers consistent.

takeaways: Your profile must show what you sell, where, why to trust you and how to order
Switch to business or professional accounts to unlock Insights, contact buttons and ads
Put a wa.me WhatsApp link in every bio
Meta Business Suite manages Facebook and Instagram posts, messages and Insights together
Turn on two-factor authentication and ignore fake support messages

activity.title: Build your shop front
steps: Switch your Instagram or TikTok to a business or professional account.
Rewrite your bio using the formula: who, result, product, place, proof, how to order.
Create your wa.me link and add it to every profile.
In WhatsApp Business, add at least five products to the catalogue and set a greeting message.
Turn on two-factor authentication on every account.
activity.evidence: Before and after screenshots of your profile and a screenshot of your WhatsApp Business catalogue.

lessons.title: How the feeds decide who sees your posts
objectives: Explain in plain words what a ranking algorithm does
Name the main signals Facebook, Instagram and TikTok use to rank content
Identify actions that help or hurt your reach
Plan posts that encourage saves, shares and replies

blocks.text: An **algorithm** is the set of rules an app uses to decide which posts to show each person, and in what order. Every user could see thousands of posts each day, so the app ranks them and shows what it predicts that person is most likely to watch, like, comment on or share. Nobody outside the companies knows the exact formulas, and they change often. But Meta and TikTok have both published explanations of the general signals they use, and those are worth understanding.
The signals, in plain words

items: **Your relationship with the viewer:** people who have messaged, commented on or watched you before are more likely to see you again.
**How people react to the post:** early watching, comments, shares and saves tell the app the post is worth showing to more people.
**Information about the post:** what it is about, when it was posted, whether it is a video, photo or text, and its caption and sounds.
**The viewer's own habits:** if she usually watches Reels about cooking, she is shown more cooking.

blocks.text: TikTok works a little differently from Facebook. Its **For You** feed mainly recommends videos based on what each person watches and interacts with, so a new account with few followers can still reach many people if a video holds attention. On Facebook and Instagram, followers and past interaction matter more for regular feed posts, while Reels are also recommended to people who do not follow you.

blocks.name: mobile-feed
blocks.alt: A phone showing a scrolling social media feed
blocks.caption: Every feed is a ranked list: the app predicts what each person will watch and interact with.

blocks.title: The reach loop
items: Post shown to small group
People watch and react
App reads the signals
Shown to more people
blocks.caption: Strong early reactions from a first small audience push a post out to a bigger audience; weak reactions slow it down.

blocks.text: What helps and what hurts

head: Usually helps reach
Usually hurts reach
rows: A strong first two seconds in videos
Slow intros and logos before anything happens
Posts people save to use later (price lists, tips, recipes)
Posts that only say "Buy now" every day
Replying to comments quickly, which creates conversation
Asking people to "comment YES" just for engagement, which platforms say they demote
Reposting other people's content or videos with another app's watermark
Posting consistently at a pace you can keep
Long silences, then many posts at once
Buying fake followers or likes, which damages trust and reach

blocks.title: Worked example: reading what the feed is telling you
blocks.context: For example, Halima sells home-made zobo and tiger-nut drinks in Kaduna. In one week she posts three things on Instagram: a flyer with prices, a carousel of "5 ways to serve zobo at a party", and a 15-second Reel of her pouring chilled zobo over ice.
steps: She opens Insights for each post after three days.
The flyer reached about 120 accounts with 2 saves. The carousel reached about 400 accounts with 35 saves. The Reel reached about 1,900 accounts, mostly non-followers, with 14 shares.
She notes the carousel was saved because it was useful, and the Reel travelled because it was visual and short.
She decides to post one useful carousel and two short Reels each week, and to put prices in a pinned post and a Highlight instead of daily flyers.
blocks.result: Halima stops guessing. She uses her own Insights to see which formats the feed rewards for her audience and plans more of those.

blocks.text: Turning signals into a posting habit

You cannot control the algorithm, but you can control what you give it. Three habits work across all platforms. First, **make every post easy to react to**: ask a real question in the caption, such as "Which colour would you wear to a wedding?", rather than "Comment YES". Second, **stay around after posting**. Spend 10 to 15 minutes replying to the first comments, because early conversation is a positive signal. Third, **make the first moment count**: the first line of a caption and the first seconds of a video decide whether people stop.

Also remember that each platform keeps adjusting how it ranks posts. When reach drops suddenly for a week, do not panic or delete posts. Check whether your posting pattern or content changed, look at what is working for similar accounts, and keep testing for at least two or three weeks before drawing conclusions.

blocks.title: Do not chase every rumour
blocks.text: You will hear claims like "post exactly at 7 pm" or "links kill your reach". Treat them as ideas to test, not rules. Your own Insights after a few weeks are more reliable than any general tip.

blocks.title: Never buy followers
blocks.text: Bought followers do not buy from you, and they do not react to your posts. Because the app first shows your post to some followers, fake ones make every post look unpopular and can reduce reach. They also break platform rules.

takeaways: Algorithms rank posts by predicting what each person will watch and interact with
Early watching, shares, saves and real comments push posts to more people
TikTok's For You feed can reach non-followers even for new accounts
Engagement bait and bought followers hurt more than they help
Your own Insights are better than general rules

activity.title: Audit your last nine posts
steps: Open Insights for your last nine posts on your main platform.
For each one write: format, reach, saves, shares and comments.
Circle the three posts with the most saves plus shares.
Write what those three have in common (format, topic, length, first seconds).
Plan two new posts that copy that pattern.
activity.evidence: A simple table of nine posts with reach, saves, shares and comments, and your two planned posts.

lessons.title: Growing a real audience without paying for it
objectives: Build a weekly content plan using content pillars
Use hashtags, keywords and location tags sensibly
Grow through collaborations, groups and customer content
Track follower growth and enquiries each month

blocks.text: **Organic growth** means growing without paying for ads. It is slower than paid ads, but it builds a group of people who know and trust you, and it costs time rather than money. The method is simple: post useful content consistently, make it easy for the right people to find you, and talk to people as a human being.
Content pillars: never run out of ideas
A **content pillar** is a theme you return to again and again. Most small businesses need three to five pillars. Mixing them stops your page from becoming a wall of adverts, which people ignore.

head: Pillar
Purpose
Example for a tailoring business
rows: Give useful tips so people save and share
How to measure yourself for a dress
Fabric to finished gown in 20 seconds
Customer photo and review, shared with permission
Show the person behind the brand
A busy Friday in the shop before a wedding weekend
New styles available, order by Wednesday for Saturday delivery

blocks.title: A healthy content mix
items: Offers (smallest share)
Proof and reviews
Show the work
Teach and entertain (largest share)
blocks.caption: Most posts should give value or build trust; direct selling posts sit on top and work better because of the posts underneath.

blocks.name: followers
blocks.alt: People connected to a profile as followers
blocks.caption: Followers grow when your posts are useful, consistent and easy to find.

blocks.text: Be easy to find

items: **Keywords:** people now search on Instagram and TikTok like a search engine. Put words like "Ankara dresses Abuja" in your name field, bio and captions.
**Hashtags:** use a few specific ones (for example #AbujaFashion, #LagosCaterer) rather than 30 general ones. Specific tags reach people who are actually looking.
**Location tags:** tag your city or area on posts, especially if you deliver locally.
**Alt text and captions:** describe what is in the photo so search features and people using screen readers understand it.

blocks.text: Grow with other people

items: **Collaborations:** Instagram's Collab feature lets one post appear on two accounts. Partner with a business that serves the same customer but does not compete, for example a caterer and a cake maker.
**Groups:** join local Facebook groups where your customers ask for recommendations. Follow each group's rules, answer questions helpfully, and only promote where it is allowed.
**Customer content:** ask happy customers to post and tag you. Reshare with their permission.
**WhatsApp Status and Channels:** share new posts to your Status so existing contacts see them.

blocks.title: Worked example: a realistic weekly plan
blocks.context: For example, Chioma runs a small skincare shop in Port Harcourt that sells shea butter blends. She has about 4 hours a week and uses Instagram as her main platform and Facebook as support.
steps: Sunday (1 hour): she batches content. She films two Reels and takes photos for a carousel in one session.
Monday: a Teach carousel, "How to store shea butter in Port Harcourt heat", posted to Instagram and Facebook together through Business Suite.
Wednesday: a Show the work Reel of her whipping a batch, with the caption keyword "whipped shea butter Port Harcourt".
Friday: a Proof post sharing a customer review with permission, plus an Offer line at the end with her WhatsApp link.
Every day (15 minutes): she replies to comments and messages and spends 5 minutes commenting helpfully in two local groups.
blocks.result: Chioma posts three times a week, every week, in about 4 hours. After a month she compares follower growth and the number of WhatsApp enquiries that mention Instagram.

blocks.text: A growth routine you can keep

Growth comes from small actions repeated every week. Many small business owners post and leave, then wonder why nothing happens. Social platforms are built around conversation, so the owner who comments, answers and shows up daily grows faster than the one who only posts.

items: Before posting, spend 5 minutes replying to comments on your last post.
After posting, stay for 10 minutes to answer early comments and messages.
Leave thoughtful comments on 5 posts from local customers, partners or groups (real sentences, not just emojis).
Share the new post to your WhatsApp Status and, where allowed, one relevant group.
Once a week, reshare a customer review or tagged post with permission.

blocks.text: Done three times a week, this routine takes about 30 minutes each time and builds relationships that turn into referrals and repeat orders.

blocks.title: Measure enquiries, not just followers
blocks.text: Ask every new customer "Where did you hear about us?" and tally the answers in a notebook. A page with 800 followers that brings ten orders a month is doing better than one with 8,000 followers that brings none.

blocks.title: Respect privacy
blocks.text: Always ask before posting a customer's photo, name or chat screenshot, and blur phone numbers and addresses. Under Nigeria's Data Protection Act, personal data should be used fairly and with a lawful basis such as consent.

takeaways: Organic growth comes from useful posts, consistency and real conversation
Use three to five content pillars and keep direct selling a small share
Specific keywords, hashtags and location tags help the right people find you
Collaborations, local groups and customer content multiply your reach
Track enquiries and sales, not only follower numbers

activity.title: Plan your first month
steps: Choose three to five content pillars for your business.
Write 12 post ideas, at least two for each pillar.
Pick three posting days you can keep every week.
List five specific hashtags and two keywords for your city and product.
Name one non-competing business you could collaborate with and draft a short message to them.
activity.evidence: A one-month content calendar with 12 ideas, your hashtags and keywords, and your collaboration message.

quiz.q: Ngozi sells home-cooked lunch packs to office workers in Victoria Island and has very little time. Which plan is best?
options: Open accounts on six platforms and post when she can
Post only on LinkedIn because office workers use it
Pick one main platform and one support platform, and send all enquiries to WhatsApp Business
Wait until she can afford an agency
quiz.explain: A small business with limited time should do one main and one support platform well, and close sales in one WhatsApp Business inbox.

quiz.q: Which bio does the best job for a business profile?
options: "Fresh small chops for parties in Ibadan. 200+ events served. Order on WhatsApp below."
"Blessed and highly favoured. DM for more."
"Welcome to my page, follow for more"
quiz.explain: It says what is sold, where, gives a proof point and explains how to order.

quiz.q: Halima's useful carousel got many saves and her flyer got almost none. What should she learn from this?
options: Her audience values useful content, so she should make more of it
quiz.explain: Saves show people found the post useful enough to keep, which is a strong signal to the feed and a clue about what to make more of.

quiz.q: Why can a brand new TikTok account still reach many people?
options: TikTok shows every video to all users
The For You feed recommends videos mainly by what people watch and interact with, not only by follower count
New accounts are given free ads
TikTok only ranks by posting time
quiz.explain: TikTok's For You feed recommends based on viewer behaviour, so a video that holds attention can travel beyond followers.

quiz.q: Which content mix follows the pyramid in this module?
options: Mostly teaching and showing the work, some reviews, and a smaller number of offers
quiz.explain: Value and trust posts form the base; direct offers are the smallest share and work better because of the posts beneath them.

quiz.q: Someone messages your business page saying they are from Meta and need your login code to give you a verified badge. What should you do?
options: Send the code quickly before the offer ends
Send your password instead of the code
Ask them to call you first, then send the code
Ignore and report the message, and never share login codes
quiz.explain: Meta does not ask for login codes in messages. This is a common account takeover scam.

modules.title: Content That Converts
modules.overview: Learn which post formats work for which goals, make simple phone videos and Reels that hold attention, use Stories and Live sessions to build trust, and turn comments and messages into sales through good community management.

lessons.title: Post formats, captions and a content calendar
objectives: Match single images, carousels, videos and text posts to a goal
Use the correct image sizes for feeds and Stories
Write captions with a hook, value and a clear call to action
Schedule a week of posts in Meta Business Suite

blocks.text: Every post should have one job. Some posts help people **discover** you, some build **trust**, and some ask for the **sale**. The format you choose and the words you write should match that job. A beautiful photo with no caption telling people what to do next wastes the attention it earned.
Formats and what they are good for

head: Format
Best job
Recommended size
Tip
rows: Show one product or announce one thing
Square 1080 x 1080 or portrait 1080 x 1350 pixels
Portrait takes up more of the phone screen
Teach a process, show a range, before and after
Slide 1 is the hook; the last slide is the call to action
Reach new people, demonstrate a product
Keep text away from the very top and bottom where buttons sit
Disappears after 24 hours unless saved to Highlights
Questions, opinions, announcements on Facebook, X or LinkedIn

blocks.name: social-media-carousel
blocks.alt: A carousel of social media post slides
blocks.caption: A carousel teaches step by step, with the hook on slide one and the call to action on the last slide.

blocks.text: Writing captions that sell

A strong caption has three parts. The **hook** is the first line, the only part people see before tapping "more", so it must make them want to read on. The **value** is the useful middle: details, benefits, a short story or tips. The **call to action** (CTA) tells them exactly what to do next: "Send 'TRAY' on WhatsApp to get the price list", "Save this for your next party", "Tag a friend who is planning a wedding".

items: Weak hook: "Good morning everyone." Strong hook: "Your jollof is not watery because of the rice. It is the tomatoes."
Write the way you speak to a customer. Short sentences. Simple words. Pidgin or local language is fine if your customers use it.
Mention price ranges or "from" prices where you can. Many buyers skip posts that only say "DM for price".
Use one CTA per post. Two or three CTAs confuse people.

blocks.title: Caption structure
items: Hook first line
Value in the middle
One clear call to action
blocks.caption: A caption moves the reader from stopping, to understanding, to acting.

blocks.text: Plan, batch and schedule

A **content calendar** is a simple table of what you will post and when. Plan a week or a month at once, create the photos and videos in one or two sessions (called batching), then schedule them. In **Meta Business Suite**, use Create post or Create reel, choose your Facebook Page and Instagram account, then pick Schedule instead of Publish now. The Planner view shows everything you have scheduled. TikTok also offers scheduling in its web tools for eligible accounts.

blocks.title: Worked example: one product, three formats
blocks.context: For example, Bisi makes adire tote bags in Abeokuta and sells them from 15,000 naira (approximate). She wants to launch a new indigo design this week.
steps: Monday (discover): a 12-second Reel of the bag being unfolded and packed with a laptop and water bottle. Hook on screen: "Fits a 14-inch laptop."
Wednesday (trust): a carousel of 6 slides: the dye process, the stitching, inside pockets, a customer carrying it, size details, and the CTA slide.
Friday (sale): a single portrait photo with the caption: "New indigo adire tote, from 15,000 naira (approximate). Only 10 made this batch. Send 'INDIGO' on WhatsApp to order."
On Sunday she batches all three in one 90-minute session and schedules them in Meta Business Suite for 7 pm each day.
blocks.result: One product gets three posts with three different jobs, created in one session and published automatically through the week.

blocks.text: Accessibility and clarity

Many people scroll in noisy buses, quiet offices or with poor eyesight. Make your posts easy for everyone: use large text with strong contrast (dark text on light backgrounds or the reverse), avoid putting important words over busy photos, and add alt text to images in Instagram and Facebook under advanced or accessibility settings. Write emojis sparingly, because screen readers read every one aloud.

Check every post on your own phone before publishing. Is the price readable? Is the product clearly the main subject? Is the call to action obvious? Would a customer who has never heard of you understand it in three seconds? If not, simplify. Fewer words and one clear picture almost always beat a crowded design. Finally, keep a simple folder on your phone for each week's photos and videos, named by date, so you can find and reuse your best content later.

blocks.title: Free design tools
blocks.text: Canva and CapCut both have free versions with templates sized for posts, Stories and Reels. Save your brand colours and fonts once so every post looks consistent.

takeaways: Give every post one job: discover, trust or sell
Use portrait 1080 x 1350 for feed images and 1080 x 1920 for Reels and Stories
Captions need a hook, value and one clear call to action
Batch your content and schedule it in Meta Business Suite

activity.title: Schedule your first week
steps: Choose one product or service to feature this week.
Plan three posts with different jobs: discover, trust, sell.
Write each caption with a hook, value and one CTA.
Create the visuals in one session using Canva, CapCut or your phone camera.
Schedule all three in Meta Business Suite (or your platform's scheduler).
activity.evidence: A screenshot of your Business Suite Planner (or scheduled posts) and your three captions.

lessons.title: Making short videos and Reels on your phone
objectives: Plan a short video with a hook, body and call to action
Film steady, bright and clear video with a phone
Edit a Reel with captions and music using free tools
Repurpose one video across Instagram, Facebook, TikTok and WhatsApp Status

blocks.text: Short vertical video is the format all the major platforms are pushing hardest. Reels on Instagram and Facebook and videos on TikTok are recommended to people who do not follow you, which makes them your best organic way to reach new customers. You do not need a camera crew. A clean phone lens, good light and a plan are enough.
The 3-part video plan

items: **Hook (first 1 to 3 seconds):** show the most interesting moment or say a bold line. "Watch this plain fabric become a wedding gown." Many viewers decide to keep watching or scroll within the first seconds.
**Body (5 to 40 seconds):** show the process, the result or the tip. Cut out any waiting. Each shot should be short.
**Call to action (last 2 to 3 seconds):** tell people what to do: "Order on WhatsApp, link in bio."

blocks.title: A 20-second Reel
items: 0-2s: hook
2-17s: show the process
17-20s: call to action
blocks.caption: Most of the time goes to showing, but the hook and the call to action decide whether people watch and act.

blocks.name: content-creator
blocks.alt: A woman recording a video with her phone
blocks.caption: A phone, good light and a plan are all you need to make Reels that reach new customers.

blocks.text: Filming basics

items: Wipe the phone lens with a soft cloth. Fingerprints make video look foggy.
Film vertically (phone upright) for Reels, TikTok and Stories.
Face a window or film outside in shade. Avoid strong light behind you, which turns you into a shadow. A ring light helps at night.
Keep the phone steady: rest it on a stack of books, a tripod or against a wall.
Record sound close to the speaker. A cheap clip-on microphone improves voice a lot. If it is noisy, add captions and music instead of speaking.
Film more short clips than you need, 3 to 5 seconds each, so editing is easy.

blocks.text: Editing and posting

You can edit inside the Instagram or TikTok app, or use **CapCut**, which has a free version. Add on-screen text for the hook, auto-captions so people can follow with the sound off, and music. Use music from the app's own library, because copyrighted songs added from elsewhere can get your video muted or blocked, and business accounts often have a more limited commercial music library. Choose a cover image that shows the product clearly, because it appears on your profile grid.

blocks.title: Worked example: a product demo Reel
blocks.context: For example, Esther sells blenders and kitchen gadgets from a small shop in Onitsha. She wants a video that shows her best-selling blender is strong enough for tiger nuts.
steps: Hook (2 seconds): close-up of hard dry tiger nuts poured into the jar, text on screen: "Can it blend tiger nuts?"
Body (12 seconds): four 3-second clips: lid closing, blender running, smooth milk being poured through a sieve, a glass of tiger-nut milk.
CTA (3 seconds): text: "Available in Onitsha. Delivery across Anambra. WhatsApp link in bio."
She edits in CapCut, adds auto-captions and a track from the app library, and posts to Instagram as a Reel shared to Facebook.
She downloads the version without the Instagram watermark from CapCut and posts it separately on TikTok and her WhatsApp Status.
blocks.result: One 17-second video, filmed in 20 minutes, now works on four channels and answers the question customers ask most.

blocks.text: Reading your video results

Video analytics tell you exactly where people lose interest. On TikTok and in Instagram Reels Insights, look at **average watch time** and, where shown, the **retention graph** that shows how many viewers are still watching at each second. A sharp drop in the first two seconds means your hook is weak. A slow fade in the middle means the body is too long or repetitive. Lots of replays mean the video is satisfying or useful to watch again.

items: Low views and low watch time: improve the hook and the cover image.
Good watch time but few profile visits: add a clearer reason to visit, such as "See prices in my bio".
Many shares: make more videos on the same topic; people find it worth passing on.
Many comments asking the same question: answer it in your next video.

blocks.text: Give each video a few days before judging it, and compare it with your own past videos, not with famous creators.
Keep your raw clips after posting. A 30-second video can later become a 7-second teaser, a Story, or part of an ad, so a folder of good clips saves hours of filming.

blocks.title: Video ideas that never run out
blocks.text: Answer one customer question per video. Show before and after. Show packing an order. Compare two products. Show a common mistake and the fix. Each of these can be filmed in under 30 minutes.

blocks.title: Do not repost with another app's watermark
blocks.text: Post the clean file from your editor on each platform. Videos carrying a visible watermark from a different app may be shown to fewer people.

takeaways: Short vertical video is the strongest organic way to reach new people
Plan every video as hook, body and call to action
Good light, a steady phone and clear sound matter more than an expensive camera
Use music from the app's library and add captions for viewers with sound off
Repurpose the clean file across Reels, TikTok and WhatsApp Status

activity.title: Make your first Reel
steps: Choose one customer question to answer in a video.
Write your hook, body shots and CTA on paper.
Film 6 to 10 short vertical clips in good light.
Edit to 15 to 30 seconds with captions and app-library music.
Post it on your main platform and share the clean file to one other channel.
activity.evidence: Your written video plan and a link or screenshot of the posted Reel with its view count after 3 days.

lessons.title: Stories, Live sessions and WhatsApp Status
objectives: Use Stories features such as polls, questions, links and countdowns
Organise Highlights so new visitors find key information
Plan and host a short Live session that sells
Use WhatsApp Status and Channels to reach existing contacts

blocks.text: Stories are short photos or videos that disappear after 24 hours. Because they feel casual and temporary, they are perfect for everyday updates, behind-the-scenes moments and quick offers. The people who watch your Stories are usually your warmest audience: people who already follow you and care what you do. That makes Stories a strong place to sell.
Story tools worth using

head: Sticker or feature
What it does
Business use
rows: "Which colour should we restock: wine or emerald?"
Collect questions, then answer them in later Stories
Send people to your WhatsApp, website or order form
Launches, end of a promo, a Live session
Saves Stories on your profile permanently
Prices, reviews, how to order, delivery areas, FAQs

blocks.text: Interactive stickers help in two ways. They tell you what your customers think, and every reply opens a direct message conversation, which is a natural moment to help and sell. Post a few Stories most days rather than 30 at once, because people tap away from long chains.

blocks.name: broadcast
blocks.alt: A person broadcasting live to an audience
blocks.caption: Live sessions let customers see you, ask questions in real time and buy with confidence.

blocks.text: Live sessions

A **Live** is a real-time video on Facebook, Instagram or TikTok. Viewers can comment and ask questions while you speak. Lives build trust quickly because people see the real product and the real person, and replays can keep getting views afterwards. TikTok sets eligibility rules for going live, such as a minimum age and follower requirements, so check the current rules in the app.

items: Announce the Live 2 to 3 days ahead with a countdown sticker.
Plan 3 to 5 talking points and keep products within reach.
Test your internet and light, and charge your phone. Use a tripod.
Start by welcoming people by name and saying what they will see.
Show products closely, repeat prices often, and explain how to order.
Pin a comment with your WhatsApp link and answer questions by name.
After the Live, message everyone who asked a question.

blocks.title: A 20-minute selling Live
items: Announce 3 days before
0-3 min: welcome
3-15 min: show products
15-20 min: questions and offer
After: follow up
blocks.caption: The work before and after the Live matters as much as the Live itself.

blocks.title: Worked example: a Thursday Live for a fabric seller
blocks.context: For example, Kemi sells lace and Ankara fabric in Lagos. Her Stories get about 300 views a day (illustrative), mostly from returning customers.
steps: Monday: she posts a countdown sticker for "New lace arrivals Live, Thursday 8 pm" and a poll asking which colours people want to see.
Thursday: she goes Live on Instagram for 20 minutes, holding each fabric to the light and stating prices per 5 yards each time.
She pins a comment with her WhatsApp link and says, "Send the fabric number and your address on WhatsApp."
During the Live, viewers reserve fabrics in the comments. Afterwards she messages each person and confirms payment in her bank app before packing.
She saves the Live clips into a Highlight called "New arrivals".
blocks.result: Customers who could not visit her shop saw the fabric move in real light, asked questions and ordered on WhatsApp the same evening.

blocks.text: WhatsApp Status and Channels

Your **WhatsApp Status** is seen by contacts who have saved your number, so ask every customer to save it. Post new arrivals, reviews and offers there. **WhatsApp Channels** are one-way broadcasts people can follow for updates. Keep both useful, not just daily flyers.
What to post in Stories each day

If you are unsure what to share, use a simple daily pattern: one behind-the-scenes moment (packing orders, the market run, a new delivery), one value item (a tip, a customer question answered) and, two or three times a week, one clear offer with a link sticker. Add text to every Story, because many people watch with sound off. Keep each video Story short and clear, and show your face sometimes, because people buy from people they feel they know.
Reshare Stories where customers tag you, after checking they are happy with it. These tagged Stories are free social proof and also remind the customer that you appreciated them.

Highlights deserve a little design care. Use simple covers in your brand colour with one-word labels such as Prices, Reviews, Order, Delivery and New. Put the most important one first, because many visitors only tap the first two. Remove outdated Stories from Highlights when prices or offers change, so customers never argue about an old price they saw on your profile.

blocks.title: Confirm payment before you ship
blocks.text: During busy Lives, fake payment screenshots and fake bank alerts are common. Only release goods after you see the money in your own bank or payment app, never because of a screenshot or SMS alone.

takeaways: Stories reach your warmest audience and work well for selling
Polls, questions and links start private conversations
Highlights keep prices, reviews and how to order on your profile permanently
Announce Lives in advance, show products closely and follow up afterwards
Confirm payment in your own bank app before shipping

activity.title: Run a Stories week
steps: Post Stories on at least five days this week, using one poll and one question box.
Create three Highlights: Prices, Reviews, How to order.
Plan a 15 to 20 minute Live with 3 to 5 talking points and announce it with a countdown.
After the Live, follow up every question in direct messages or WhatsApp.
activity.evidence: Screenshots of your poll results, your three Highlights, and notes on how many enquiries came from the Live.

lessons.title: Turning comments and messages into customers
objectives: Reply to comments and messages in a way that moves people towards buying
Organise WhatsApp Business chats with labels and quick replies
Handle complaints and negative comments calmly in public
Set clear response times and a simple customer service routine

blocks.text: **Community management** means looking after the people who interact with your business online: replying to comments, answering messages, handling complaints and encouraging conversation. For a small business, this is where most sales are actually won. A customer who asks "How much?" and waits two days for a reply often buys from someone else.
Reply in a way that sells

items: **Answer the question first.** If someone asks the price, give the price or price range. Then invite the next step.
**Use their name** and keep a warm, respectful tone.
**Move buying conversations to private chat:** "The medium size is 12,000 naira (approximate). I have sent you photos on WhatsApp."
**Reply to every genuine comment,** even with a short thank you. Replies create conversation, which helps the post reach more people.
**Pin helpful comments** or your own comment with ordering details.

blocks.name: social-media-interactions
blocks.alt: People exchanging comments and likes on social media
blocks.caption: Every comment and message is a chance to help someone take the next step towards buying.

blocks.text: Organise your inbox

Use the **Meta Business Suite inbox** to answer Facebook and Instagram messages and comments in one place, and set automatic replies such as an instant greeting and FAQs. In **WhatsApp Business**, use **labels** (for example New enquiry, Awaiting payment, Paid, Delivered) so you can see where every customer is. Save **quick replies** for your price list, delivery fees and account details. Set an **away message** for outside working hours that says when you will reply.

blocks.title: From enquiry to repeat customer
items: New enquiry
Answer and send options
Awaiting payment
Paid and delivered
Follow up for review
blocks.caption: Labels in WhatsApp Business let you move each customer through these stages without losing anyone.

blocks.text: Handling complaints and negative comments

items: Do not delete honest complaints or argue in public. Other customers are watching how you respond.
Reply quickly and calmly in public: thank them, apologise for the experience, and invite them to private chat to solve it.
In private, listen, ask for the order details, and offer a fair fix: replacement, repair, partial refund or credit.
When it is solved, it is fine to reply publicly that it has been resolved.
Do hide or delete spam, insults, scams and comments that share private information, and block repeat abusers.

blocks.title: Worked example: rescuing a public complaint
blocks.context: For example, Amaka runs a cake business in Enugu. A customer comments under her latest post: "My cake arrived with the top crushed. Very disappointing."
steps: Within an hour, Amaka replies publicly: "I am so sorry, Nkechi. That is not the standard we aim for. I have sent you a message so we can make this right today."
In WhatsApp she asks for a photo, the order date and the delivery time, and learns the rider was delayed in traffic for two hours on a hot afternoon.
She offers a free replacement cake for the next week or a 50 percent refund. Nkechi chooses the replacement.
Amaka changes her delivery process: insulated boxes and no cake deliveries left in vehicles for long periods.
After the replacement, Nkechi updates her comment to say the issue was resolved.
blocks.result: A public complaint became public proof of good service, and Amaka fixed the real cause so it does not happen again.

blocks.text: Building a community, not just a customer list

Customers who feel part of something come back and bring friends. Simple ways to build that feeling: celebrate customers (with permission) in a weekly "customer of the week" post, ask for opinions before launching new products, reply to Stories that mention you, and thank repeat customers by name. A WhatsApp Channel or a small Facebook Group for loyal customers can share early access to new stock or special offers.

Write down your house rules for comments, for example no insults, no spam links, no sharing other people's private information. Pin them if you run a group. Clear rules make it easier to remove abuse fairly and keep the space pleasant for everyone. Also decide who answers messages when you are ill, travelling or busy; even a trusted family member with saved quick replies is better than silence for days.

Measure your service as well as your posts. Each week, note how many enquiries you received, how quickly you replied on average, and how many enquiries became orders. If many people ask the price and then go silent, test sending photos and the delivery fee together in your first reply, or offering two clear options instead of one. Small changes in how you reply often lift sales more than new posts do.

blocks.title: Set a response time and keep it
blocks.text: Decide on a reply time you can keep, for example within 2 hours between 8 am and 8 pm. Put your hours in your profile and away message. Consistent replies build trust faster than clever posts.

blocks.title: Protect customer data
blocks.text: Never post a customer's phone number, address or payment details in comments. Use private chat for anything personal, and do not share chat screenshots without blurring personal information.

takeaways: Most small business sales are won or lost in comments and messages
Answer the question, then invite the next step in private chat
Use labels, quick replies and away messages in WhatsApp Business
Respond to complaints publicly and calmly, then solve them privately
Remove spam and abuse, never honest criticism

activity.title: Set up your customer service routine
steps: Create five WhatsApp Business labels for the stages of your sales process.
Save at least four quick replies: prices, delivery, payment details, thank you.
Set a greeting message and an away message with your working hours.
Write a short template for replying to a public complaint.
For one week, record how long it takes you to reply to each enquiry.
activity.evidence: Screenshots of your labels and quick replies, your complaint template, and your one-week reply-time log.

quiz.q: Bisi wants a post that teaches how her adire bags are dyed, step by step. Which format fits best?
options: A carousel with one step per slide
quiz.explain: Carousels are ideal for teaching a process, with a hook on slide one and the call to action on the last slide.

quiz.q: Which caption opening is the strongest hook?
options: "Your jollof is not watery because of the rice. It is the tomatoes."
quiz.explain: A hook should make people curious enough to keep reading. A surprising, specific claim does that.

quiz.q: Esther's Reel has a slow 6-second logo intro and gets few views. What should she change first?
options: Start with the most interesting moment in the first 1 to 3 seconds
quiz.explain: Viewers decide quickly whether to keep watching. A strong hook at the start matters most.

quiz.q: During a Live, a viewer sends a screenshot showing she has paid. What should Kemi do before shipping?
options: Check that the money has arrived in her own bank or payment app
Ship immediately because the screenshot looks real
quiz.explain: Fake screenshots and alerts are common. Only confirm payment in your own bank or payment app.

quiz.q: A customer posts an honest complaint under your post. What is the best first step?
options: Argue that it is not your fault
Reply calmly in public, apologise and move to private chat to fix it
quiz.explain: Other customers watch how you respond. A calm public reply followed by a private fix builds trust.

quiz.q: Which WhatsApp Business feature helps you see which customers still need to pay?
quiz.explain: Labels let you sort chats by stage so nobody gets lost between enquiry and delivery.

modules.title: Paid Social Advertising
modules.overview: Move from boosting posts to running simple, controlled ads in Meta Ads Manager. Learn campaign structure, targeting and retargeting, ad creative and copy, and how to set small naira budgets and judge whether an ad is making money.

lessons.title: Boost or Ads Manager: how Meta ads are built
objectives: Explain the difference between boosting a post and using Ads Manager
Describe the campaign, ad set and ad structure
Choose a campaign objective that matches a business goal
Run a small Click-to-WhatsApp boost safely

blocks.text: Paid social means paying a platform to show your content to more people, or to specific people. On Facebook and Instagram there are two main ways to do it. **Boosting** turns an existing post into an ad with a few taps. **Meta Ads Manager** (adsmanager.facebook.com) is the full tool with more control over goals, audiences, placements and testing. Start with boosting, then move to Ads Manager once you want more control.

head: Boost a post
Ads Manager
rows: "Boost" button on a Page or Instagram post, or in Business Suite
adsmanager.facebook.com or the Ads Manager app
A short list such as more messages, more profile visits, more engagement
Six campaign objectives with detailed settings
Several ad sets and ads compared side by side
Pushing a post that is already doing well

blocks.name: online-ad
blocks.alt: An advert displayed on a web page and phone
blocks.caption: A boost or an ad pays to put your best content in front of the people most likely to buy.

blocks.text: The three levels of every Meta campaign

blocks.title: Campaign structure
items: Ads: images, video, text
Ad sets: audience, budget, schedule
Campaign: one objective
blocks.caption: One campaign has one objective; inside it, ad sets decide who and how much, and ads are what people actually see.

items: **Campaign:** you choose one objective. Meta's objectives are Awareness, Traffic, Engagement, Leads, App promotion and Sales.
**Ad set:** you choose the audience, placements (Facebook, Instagram, Messenger and others), budget and schedule.
**Ad:** the creative (image or video), the text, the headline and the button, such as Send message or Shop now.

blocks.text: Picking the right objective

head: Your goal
Objective to consider
rows: Get more WhatsApp or Messenger chats from buyers
Engagement (messages) or Sales with a messaging destination
More people to know your brand in your city
Visits to your website or online store
Collect names and numbers for a class or service
Purchases on your website with the Meta Pixel installed

blocks.text: For most Nigerian small businesses that close sales in chat, a **Click-to-WhatsApp** ad is the natural first step: people tap the button and a WhatsApp chat with your business opens. Connect your WhatsApp Business number to your Facebook Page first (in Page settings under linked accounts).

blocks.title: Worked example: a first boost for messages
blocks.context: For example, Grace sells frozen chicken and turkey in Abuja. Her Reel showing her cold room and clean packaging already has more comments than usual.
steps: She taps Boost on the Reel and chooses the goal "Get more messages", with WhatsApp as the destination.
Audience: people aged 25 to 55 within about 15 km of her shop (the area she delivers to).
Budget: about 2,000 naira per day (approximate) for 5 days, a total of about 10,000 naira.
She adds a quick reply in WhatsApp Business for the price list so she can answer every new chat within minutes.
After 5 days she records spend, number of new conversations and number of orders from those chats.
blocks.result: Grace learns her real cost per conversation and cost per order before spending more, instead of guessing.

blocks.text: Before you spend your first naira

items: **Promote proven content.** Pay to push a post that is already getting comments, shares or saves organically. Ads amplify; they rarely rescue a weak post.
**Be ready for replies.** Ads that bring messages nobody answers waste money. Plan to reply within minutes during the ad period.
**Know your numbers.** Know your price, your profit per order and how many enquiries usually turn into orders (Lesson 3.4).
**Start small and time-limited.** Run a test for 5 to 7 days with a fixed amount you can afford to lose while learning.
**Set up Business Manager access.** In Meta Business Settings (part of Business Suite), add your Page, Instagram account, ad account and WhatsApp number, and give any helper their own role.

blocks.text: You can also look at the Meta **Ad Library**, a free public search tool, to see the ads that other businesses in your industry are running right now. It is a good source of ideas for formats and offers, though you should never copy someone else's photos or words.

blocks.title: Know the ad rules
blocks.text: Meta reviews every ad against its Advertising Standards. Some products are restricted or banned, and credit, employment, housing and social or political ads have special rules. In Nigeria, ARCON regulates advertising, and regulated products such as food, drugs and cosmetics must not make unapproved health claims. Never claim a product cures a disease.

blocks.title: Pay only through Meta
blocks.text: Add your payment method only inside Ads Manager or Business Suite billing. Be careful with people who offer to "run your ads cheaply" if you send them money or your login. Use Business Settings to give a helper their own access instead of sharing your password.

takeaways: Boosting is quick; Ads Manager gives more control and testing
Every campaign has one objective, ad sets choose audience and budget, ads are the creative
Click-to-WhatsApp ads suit businesses that close sales in chat
Follow Meta's ad rules and never make unapproved health claims
Give helpers access through Business Settings, never your password

activity.title: Prepare your first ad
steps: Pick one post from the last month that got more comments or shares than usual.
Write your goal in one line, for example "20 new WhatsApp chats from buyers in my delivery area".
Choose the matching objective from the table.
Connect your WhatsApp Business number to your Facebook Page.
Write down your planned audience, daily budget and number of days.
activity.evidence: A one-page ad plan with the chosen post, goal, objective, audience, budget and duration.

lessons.title: Targeting the right people and retargeting warm audiences
objectives: Build a location, age and interest audience for a local business
Explain custom audiences and lookalike audiences
Set up a retargeting audience of people who engaged with you
Avoid audiences that are too narrow or too broad

blocks.text: Targeting means choosing who should see your ad. Good targeting puts your money in front of people who can actually buy: they live where you deliver, can afford your product, and are interested in what you sell. Meta offers three main types of audience.

head: Audience type
What it is
Example
rows: Built from location, age, gender, language and interests
Women 25 to 50 in Lekki, interested in fashion and weddings
People who already know you: engaged with your Page or Instagram, watched your videos, visited your website, or are on a customer list
People who watched at least half of your Reels in the last 90 days
New people similar to a custom audience you choose
People in Nigeria who resemble your past buyers

blocks.name: target
blocks.alt: A target with an arrow in the centre
blocks.caption: Targeting focuses your budget on people who can actually buy from you.

blocks.text: Building a local audience

items: **Location first.** Choose the city, or drop a pin and set a radius covering only the areas you can deliver to or serve.
**Age range** that matches your real buyers, from your customer list or Insights.
**Interests** related to your product, for example cooking, weddings, skincare or small business. Start with a few and let the system find people.
**Check the estimated audience size** shown on the right of the screen. If it is very small, results can be slow and expensive; if it is huge and your product is local, check your location.

Meta's **Advantage+ audience** option lets the system widen beyond your suggestions when it predicts better results. It often works well once you have some data, but keep location limits that matter for delivery.

blocks.text: Retargeting: your most profitable audience

**Retargeting** means showing ads to people who have already interacted with you. They know your name, so they are much more likely to respond than strangers. In Ads Manager, go to Audiences, create a Custom audience, and choose a source such as Instagram account, Facebook Page or Video. For example: everyone who sent you a message or engaged with your Instagram in the last 60 days. If you have a website, install the **Meta Pixel** so you can retarget people who visited product pages.

blocks.title: Cold to warm to buyer
items: Cold: strangers see a Reel
Warm: they watch or engage
Retarget with an offer
Buyer messages and pays
blocks.caption: Spend some budget finding new people, and some showing a clear offer to those who already showed interest.

blocks.title: Worked example: two audiences for a hair business
blocks.context: For example, Joy sells hair extensions and wigs in Port Harcourt and delivers within Rivers State. She has a budget of about 21,000 naira (approximate) for one week.
steps: Ad set 1 (cold): women 22 to 45 in Rivers State, interests in hair care and beauty salons, about 1,500 naira per day. The ad is a Reel showing a wig being installed.

Ad set 2 (warm, retargeting): a custom audience of people who engaged with her Instagram or watched her videos in the last 60 days, about 1,500 naira per day. The ad is a photo carousel with prices and a "Send WhatsApp message" button.
After 7 days: the cold ad set brought 28 conversations at about 375 naira each; the warm ad set brought 42 conversations at about 250 naira each.
Joy notes that warm conversations also turned into orders more often, so next week she keeps both but watches the cost per order, not only cost per chat.
blocks.result: Joy sees that retargeting brings cheaper and better chats, while the cold ad set keeps filling her warm audience with new people. The figures are illustrative.

blocks.text: Mistakes that waste ad money

items: **Targeting all of Nigeria when you only deliver in one city.** You pay for messages you cannot serve.
**Stacking many narrow interests** until the audience is tiny. Results slow down and costs rise.
**Choosing an age range from guesswork.** Check your customer records or Insights first.
**Showing the same ad to the same people for weeks.** Watch **frequency** (the average number of times each person has seen the ad). When it climbs high and results fall, refresh the creative.
**Running cold and warm audiences with the same message.** Strangers need an introduction; warm audiences need a clear offer.

blocks.text: Keep a simple note of every audience you test, with the cost per result and number of orders it brought. Over a few months, this note becomes your most valuable guide to where your buyers really are.

blocks.title: Customer lists and privacy
blocks.text: If you upload a customer list for a custom audience, only use contacts who gave you their details and would reasonably expect to hear from you. Meta hashes the data for matching, but you are still responsible for collecting it fairly under Nigeria's Data Protection Act.

blocks.title: Exclude recent buyers
blocks.text: When running an offer for new customers, exclude a custom audience of people who already bought, so you do not pay to show them an ad for something they have.

takeaways: Location should match where you can actually deliver or serve
Custom audiences are people who already know you; lookalikes are new people like them
Retargeting warm audiences is often the most profitable spend
Watch the estimated audience size: not too narrow, not wastefully broad
Use customer data fairly and exclude people who have already bought

activity.title: Build two audiences
steps: In Ads Manager, open Audiences.
Create a saved audience with your delivery location, age range and three interests.
Create a custom audience of people who engaged with your Instagram or Facebook Page in the last 60 or 90 days.
Note the estimated size of each audience.
Write which ad you would show to each one and why.
activity.evidence: Screenshots of both audiences with their settings and size, and your note on which ad suits each.

lessons.title: Ad creative and copy that people respond to
objectives: Design an ad image or video that stops the scroll
Write primary text, headline and call-to-action button that match the goal
Use offers, proof and urgency honestly
Test two versions of an ad to find the better one

blocks.text: Your targeting decides who could see the ad. Your **creative** (the picture or video) and **copy** (the words) decide whether they stop, read and act. In practice, creative is usually the part with the biggest effect on results, so it deserves most of your effort.
What makes ad creative work

items: **Native look:** ads that look like a normal post or Reel usually do better than heavy, flyer-style designs crowded with text.
**Show the product in use:** hands opening it, a person wearing it, food being served, a before and after.
**Big, short on-screen text:** three to six words that state the benefit, for example "Fresh soup delivered Saturday".
**Vertical formats:** 9:16 video for Reels and Stories, 4:5 images for feeds.
**Real faces and real customers** (with permission) build trust better than stock photos.

blocks.name: product-photography
blocks.alt: A person photographing a product on a table
blocks.caption: Clear photos and videos of the real product in use usually outperform crowded flyers.

blocks.text: The parts of an ad

head: Part
What it is
Example for a cleaning service
rows: The words above the image; the first line is the hook
"Moving out this month? We deep-clean 3-bedroom flats in one day."
Short bold line under the image
15-second before and after of a kitchen

blocks.text: A simple copy formula is **Problem, Solution, Proof, Action**. Name the problem the customer has, show how you solve it, add proof such as a review or number of happy customers you can honestly claim, then give one action. Keep the primary text short, because only the first lines show before "See more".

blocks.title: Weak ad versus strong ad
items: Weak ad
Strong ad
blocks.caption: A strong ad is specific, honest and easy to act on.

blocks.title: Worked example: testing two ads
blocks.context: For example, Uche runs a laundry and dry-cleaning service in Enugu with pickup and delivery. He has about 14,000 naira (approximate) to test ads for one week.
steps: Ad A: a designed flyer with the price list, logo and phone number. Primary text: "Quality laundry services. Call now."

Ad B: a 12-second video of a rider collecting a laundry bag, then the same clothes returned folded. Primary text: "Too busy for laundry this week? We pick up, wash, iron and return in 48 hours across Enugu." Button: Send WhatsApp message.
He runs both in the same ad set, same audience, about 1,000 naira per day each, for 7 days.
Result: Ad A brought 9 conversations (about 780 naira each). Ad B brought 31 conversations (about 225 naira each).
He turns off Ad A and makes two new versions of Ad B with different hooks to test next week.
blocks.result: By changing only the creative and copy, Uche found an ad that brought over three times as many chats for the same money. The numbers are illustrative; your results will differ.

blocks.text: Hooks that work for ads
The first line of primary text and the first seconds of video do most of the work. Here are hook patterns you can adapt honestly to your own business:

items: **Question:** "Still washing your curtains by hand every month?"
**Specific promise:** "Your wedding small chops, delivered hot in Ibadan, on time."
**Before and after:** show the problem, then the result.
**Customer voice:** a short real review read aloud or shown on screen, with permission.
**Myth buster:** "Shea butter does not go bad in two weeks. Here is how to store it."

blocks.text: Write five hooks for each new ad and test the best two. Keep a swipe file, a folder of your best-performing ads and other ads you admire from the Ad Library, so you never start from a blank page. Remember that ad creative wears out: when the same audience has seen an ad many times, results drop, and a fresh video with a new hook often brings costs back down.

Before publishing, preview your ad in every placement Ads Manager offers, such as Facebook Feed, Instagram Feed, Stories and Reels. Text that looks fine in the feed may be covered by buttons in Stories. If a placement looks wrong, upload a version made for that size or remove that placement. Also read your ad copy aloud once: if it sounds like a radio jingle rather than a person talking to a friend, simplify it.

blocks.title: Honest offers only
blocks.text: Only use claims you can prove, such as "over 200 orders delivered" if your records show it. Fake countdowns, invented discounts and before and after images that are edited or not yours break advertising rules and destroy trust.

blocks.title: Change one thing at a time
blocks.text: When testing, change only one element between versions, for example the video or the first line. Then you know what caused the difference.

takeaways: Creative usually has the biggest effect on ad results
Show the real product in use in vertical, native-looking formats
Use Problem, Solution, Proof, Action and one clear button
Test two versions, change one thing, keep the winner
Make only claims you can prove

activity.title: Create and test two ads
steps: Write your ad copy using Problem, Solution, Proof, Action.
Create two creatives: a flyer-style image and a native-style short video or real photo.
Write a headline and choose one call-to-action button.
If you have budget, run both to the same audience for at least 5 days; if not, show both to five customers and ask which makes them want to buy.
Record the result and decide which version to keep.
activity.evidence: Both ad versions (screenshots), your copy, and the results or customer feedback with your decision.

lessons.title: Small budgets in naira: spending, bidding and knowing if ads pay
objectives: Choose between daily and lifetime budgets
Explain the learning phase and common bid strategies
Calculate cost per result, cost per order and break-even cost
Decide when to pause, adjust or increase an ad

blocks.text: You do not need a big budget to learn from ads, but you do need to control spending and measure results. The question is never "How much should I spend?" alone. It is "How much can I afford to pay to get one customer, and is the ad getting customers below that amount?"
Budget types

items: **Daily budget:** the average amount spent per day. Meta may spend a bit more on some days and less on others, but keeps the weekly total in line with your daily budget.
**Lifetime budget:** a total amount over a set period, for example 15,000 naira (approximate) from Monday to Sunday. Useful for a promotion with an end date.
**Minimum budget:** Ads Manager shows the minimum allowed for your currency and objective when you set the budget, so check it there rather than relying on a figure you heard.

blocks.name: budget-adjustments
blocks.alt: A person adjusting budget sliders on a screen
blocks.caption: Set a budget you can afford to lose while learning, then adjust it based on cost per order.

blocks.text: The learning phase and bidding

When an ad set starts, or after a big change, it enters the **learning phase** while the system works out who responds. Meta explains that ad sets usually need around 50 results in a week to leave learning. Results can be unstable during this time, so avoid editing the ad every day. Small budgets may stay in learning; that is normal, so judge them over a week rather than a day.

head: Bid strategy
What it does
When to use it
rows: Gets as many results as possible for your budget
Tries to keep the average cost near a target you set
When you know your affordable cost per result
Sets the maximum bid in each auction
Aims for a set return on ad spend from purchases
Online stores tracking sales value with the Pixel

blocks.text: The numbers that matter

items: **Cost per result** = amount spent ÷ number of results (for example, conversations).
**Conversion rate** = orders ÷ conversations × 100.
**Cost per order** = amount spent ÷ orders.
**Break-even cost per order** = your profit per order before ads. If an order costs more than this in ads, you are losing money.

blocks.title: Is my ad making money?
items: Amount spent
Conversations
Orders
Cost per order
Compare with profit
blocks.caption: Follow the money from spend to orders and compare the cost per order with what each order really earns you.

blocks.title: Worked example: does the ad pay?
blocks.context: For example, Rukayat sells ready-to-cook pepper soup packs in Lagos for about 6,500 naira (approximate). After ingredients, packaging and her own delivery cost, she keeps about 2,500 naira profit per pack.
steps: She runs a Click-to-WhatsApp ad at about 2,000 naira per day for 7 days: total spend about 14,000 naira.
The ad brings 40 conversations. Cost per conversation = 14,000 ÷ 40 = 350 naira.
From those chats she gets 10 orders. Conversion rate = 10 ÷ 40 × 100 = 25 percent.
Cost per order = 14,000 ÷ 10 = 1,400 naira. Her break-even is 2,500 naira, so each order still leaves about 1,100 naira profit after ads.
Some of those 10 customers reorder later, which makes the ad even more valuable over time.
blocks.result: The ad pays. Rukayat raises the budget gradually, by about 20 percent at a time, and keeps checking that cost per order stays below 2,500 naira. All figures are illustrative.

blocks.text: A simple ad results log

head: Week
Spend (approx.)
Conversations
Orders
Cost per order
Decision
rows: Pause old creative, frequency too high

blocks.text: The log above is illustrative, but it shows how a few lines each week make decisions obvious. In week 3 the cost per order rose above break-even, so the ad needed a fresh creative. Without the log, it would be easy to keep spending on an ad that had stopped working. Record the figures from Ads Manager every week on the same day, and add the orders from your WhatsApp labels.

Remember that the cheapest result is not always the best. A campaign with cheap clicks but no orders is worse than one with costlier messages that turn into sales. Always judge by cost per order and repeat purchases.

blocks.title: When to pause or scale
blocks.text: Pause an ad if, after about a week, cost per order is clearly above your break-even. Improve the creative or offer before trying again. If it is clearly below break-even, increase the budget gradually rather than doubling it overnight, so the ad set stays stable.

blocks.title: Set a spending limit
blocks.text: In Meta billing settings you can set an account spending limit. Use it while you learn, and check your bank statements against the receipts in Billing and payments.

takeaways: Daily budgets suit ongoing ads; lifetime budgets suit dated promotions
Avoid daily edits during the learning phase and judge results over a week
Highest volume bidding is the best starting point
Cost per order must stay below your profit per order
Scale winners gradually and use an account spending limit

activity.title: Work out your break-even
steps: Choose your best-selling product and write its selling price.
Subtract all costs (materials, packaging, delivery, payment fees) to get profit per order before ads.
Estimate your conversion rate from chats to orders using last month's WhatsApp chats.
Calculate the maximum you can pay per conversation and still break even.
Plan a test budget for 7 days and the result that would make you pause or scale.
activity.evidence: A calculation sheet showing price, costs, profit per order, conversion rate, maximum cost per conversation and your test plan.

quiz.q: Grace closes most sales in WhatsApp chats. Which ad setup fits best?
options: An Awareness campaign with no button
A Traffic campaign to a website she does not have
